scale.meaning: Turing pigment stripe / ocellus wavelength on fetal Felis catus skin

evolutionary_history.what_changes: No second Felis chronospecies. At 80 µm the fundamental mode is stable (no stripe). At 436 µm the fastest Turing mode is selected. At 4360 µm the same k* is repeated ten times, so stripe number changes and the wavenumber does not.

equations: du/dt = Du * laplacian(u) + gamma * (a - u + u^2 v)
dv/dt = Dv * laplacian(v) + gamma * (b - u^2 v)
k* = argmax sigma(k), sigma = leading eigenvalue of J - k^2 D
lambda = 2*pi/k* = 436 µm at the nominal Holocene point
governing_model.boundary_conditions: periodic square patch (Turing ring/torus), spectral operator split

empirical_claims.claim: A homogeneous reaction-diffusion system can be unstable at a finite wavenumber and produce stationary waves.
Mammalian coat markings can be read as a pre-pattern whose stripe or spot count depends on domain size relative to the chemical wavelength.
Taqpep establishes a periodic pre-pattern in fetal cat skin; Edn3 later implements the pigment difference. The same gene converts cheetah spots to king-cheetah stripes.
In fetal domestic-cat skin, a Dkk4 expression pre-pattern and stripe-like epidermal thickening precede visible hair color. Dkk4 is mutated in the Ticked pattern.

does_not_claim: That 436 µm was measured by Kaelin, Murray, or Turing.
That the Schnakenberg rates are Dkk4 or Wnt biochemical constants.
That the snow photograph resolves a 436 µm primordium.

specimen.description: Domestic cat, a ten month old female tabby on snow. Vendored 1280 px rendition of the Commons original.
